laws.historical_context: Armenian Catholics are one of the six Eastern Catholic communities sharing the unified 1949 Personal Status Law. They recognize the authority of the Pope while maintaining Armenian liturgical and cultural traditions. The 1990 Code of Canons of Eastern Churches (CCEO) introduced spousal equality provisions (Canon 777) that apply to all Eastern Catholic churches. The Armenian Catholic Church has its own patriarchate and follows the Code of Procedure for Tribunals of Eastern Catholic Churches for court procedures.

annulment_grounds: Inability to contract marriage due to mental impairment or insanity
Inability to perform major marital duties toward spouse
Mental or physical incapacity preventing essential marital responsibilities

divorce_provisions.separation: Legal separation (infisal) available without right to remarry

inheritance_laws.children_share: Equal distribution among all children regardless of gender

custody_guardianship.breastfeeding_duration: 2 years - mother's exclusive right and obligation (Article 124)

laws.historical_context: Syriac Catholics are one of the six Eastern Catholic communities sharing the unified 1949 Personal Status Law. They recognize the authority of the Pope while maintaining West Syriac liturgical traditions. The 1990 Code of Canons of Eastern Churches (CCEO) introduced significant reforms including spousal equality (Canon 777). The Syriac Catholic Church has its own patriarchate (the Syriac Catholic Patriarchate of Antioch) and follows the Code of Procedure for Tribunals of Eastern Catholic Churches. The community has ancient roots in the Levant and maintains distinct cultural and religious traditions.

laws.historical_context: Chaldean Catholics are one of the six Eastern Catholic communities sharing the unified 1949 Personal Status Law. They recognize the authority of the Pope while maintaining East Syriac liturgical traditions. The 1990 Code of Canons of Eastern Churches (CCEO) introduced significant reforms including spousal equality (Canon 777). The Chaldean Catholic Church has its own patriarchate (the Chaldean Catholic Patriarchate of Babylon) based in Baghdad, with diaspora communities throughout the world including Lebanon. Many Chaldeans in Lebanon are refugees from Iraq. The community follows the Code of Procedure for Tribunals of Eastern Catholic Churches.
